callouts.label: Olympieion
callouts.hint: A huge walled precinct with a temple in its center, at the northern edge of the city.
callouts.description: The Olympieion was an enormous temple precinct built for the worship of the emperor Hadrian as Olympian Zeus, an honor that let Ephesus call itself a temple-keeper of the emperors. Little stands above the foundations, because its marble was carried off for later buildings.

callouts.label: Church of Mary
callouts.hint: A long narrow building north of the harbor complex, beside a large temple precinct.
callouts.description: The Church of Mary is a long ruined church near the old harbor, built inside an older Roman hall, and one of the first churches anywhere dedicated to Mary, the mother of Jesus. In 431 CE it hosted the Council of Ephesus, the third of the great councils of the Church, which declared Mary 'the God-bearer.'

callouts.label: Ancient Harbour
callouts.hint: The blue basin at the end of a long channel, west of the city.
callouts.description: The Ancient Harbor was the reason Ephesus grew rich, and its loss is why the city died. Mud carried down by the river Küçük Menderes, the ancient Kaystros, kept filling it in. The Romans dredged it again and again, and the long blue channel on the map is the canal that linked it to the sea. Today the harbor is a marshy field and the coast lies several kilometers to the west.
callouts.tip: Stand at the bottom of Harbor Street and look west. Everything flat in front of you was once water.

callouts.label: Harbour Gymnasium
callouts.hint: A building complex at the head of the old harbor, west of the largest courtyard.
callouts.description: The Harbor Gymnasium and Baths form the largest building complex in Ephesus, begun in the late 1st century CE beside the harbor. Like the city's other gymnasia, it combined exercise grounds, lecture rooms, and heated baths, so that a visitor stepping off a ship could bathe before entering the city.

callouts.label: Hall of Verulanus
callouts.hint: The largest square on the map, a huge walled courtyard between the theater and the harbor.
callouts.description: The Hall of Verulanus is a vast open courtyard surrounded by colonnades, the exercise ground of the Harbor Gymnasium. It is named for Claudius Verulanus, a high priest who paid to face its walls with marble in the reign of Hadrian. Athletes trained here in the open air.

callouts.label: Theatre Gymnasium
callouts.hint: A square building just north of the theater, with an open courtyard.
callouts.description: The Theater Gymnasium is a Roman bath and exercise complex just north of the Great Theater. Its large open courtyard, the palaestra, was used for wrestling and athletic training, and its heated rooms for bathing.

callouts.label: Arcadiane (Harbour Street)
callouts.hint: A straight street running west from the theater to the edge of the old harbor.
callouts.description: The Arcadiane, or Harbor Street, is a colonnaded marble street about half a kilometer long that ran from the Great Theater down to the harbor. It is named for the emperor Arcadius, who rebuilt it around 400 CE. Travelers arriving by sea walked up it into the heart of the city.

callouts.label: Great Theatre
callouts.hint: A semicircle of seats cut into the western slope of the northern hill.
callouts.description: The Great Theater is set into the western slope of Panayırdağ and faces down Harbor Street toward the old harbor. First built in the 3rd century BCE and enlarged by the Romans, it seated about 24,000 people. Acts 19 tells how silversmiths who made shrines of Artemis filled it to protest against Paul's preaching.
callouts.tip: Climb a few rows up. From here you can see how Harbor Street once ran straight to the sea.

callouts.label: Tetragonos Agora (Commercial Market)
callouts.hint: A large square courtyard surrounded by colonnades, between the library and the theater.
callouts.description: The Tetragonos Agora, Greek for 'square market,' was the city's main marketplace, a courtyard about 110 meters on a side lined with colonnades and shops. Traders sold food, cloth, slaves, and goods from across the Mediterranean here. The Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates, beside the library, leads into it.

callouts.label: Serapeion
callouts.hint: A small square temple just west of the square market, set back from the main street.
callouts.description: The Serapeion is a 2nd-century CE temple of Serapis, a god from Egypt. Its presence reflects the city's close trade with Alexandria, the grain port of Egypt. In the Christian period the temple was turned into a church.

callouts.label: Celsus Library
callouts.hint: A marker at the foot of the diagonal street, at the corner of the large square market.
callouts.description: The Library of Celsus was built around 110 to 125 CE by Tiberius Julius Aquila as a memorial to his father, Celsus, a governor of the province of Asia, who is buried in a stone coffin under the floor. Its two-story front was put back together from its fallen pieces by Austrian archaeologists in the 1970s. It is the best-known view in Ephesus.
callouts.tip: The Library of Celsus Facade poster reads the front of the building part by part.

callouts.label: Temple of Hadrian
callouts.hint: A small marker on the diagonal street that runs downhill from the upper square toward the library.
callouts.description: The Temple of Hadrian is a small, finely carved temple on Curetes Street, dedicated to the emperor Hadrian before 138 CE. Its front arch carries a bust of Tyche, goddess of the city's fortune. The relief panels inside the porch today are casts; the originals are in the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk.

callouts.label: Terrace House 2
callouts.hint: A plain marker on the hillside just south of the diagonal street, opposite a small temple.
callouts.description: Terrace House 2 is a block of wealthy Roman homes built in terraces up the slope on the south side of Curetes Street, opposite the Temple of Hadrian. It held seven family apartments, lived in from the 1st century BCE until earthquakes in the 3rd century CE. A modern roof now protects their wall paintings, marble-paneled rooms, and mosaic floors.
callouts.tip: The Terrace Houses need a separate ticket. If your tour skips them, ask where the group will meet and go in on your own for thirty to forty minutes.

callouts.label: Hellenistic City Walls
callouts.hint: A dark line running along the ridge of the southern hill, drawn around the whole city.
callouts.description: The Hellenistic City Walls were built by Lysimachus, one of Alexander the Great's successors, when he refounded Ephesus on this site around 290 BCE. They run along the ridge of Bülbüldağ and around Panayırdağ, enclosing far more land than the city ever filled. The square tower called St. Paul's Prison, on the western ridge, is part of these walls.
callouts.tip: The number 15 appears three times on the sign because the wall circles the whole city. This marker sits on the stretch along Bülbüldağ.

callouts.label: Ayasuluk Fortress
callouts.hint: A walled hilltop at the very top right corner of the map.
callouts.description: The Ayasuluk Fortress crowns the hill above Selçuk. As the harbor failed, people moved up here from the old city, and Byzantine, Aydınid, and Ottoman rulers built and rebuilt its walls. The name Ayasuluk comes from Greek words meaning 'holy theologian,' a title of St. John.

callouts.label: Basilica of St. John
callouts.hint: A cross-shaped church on the slope of the far hill in the northeast corner.
callouts.description: The Basilica of St. John is the ruined church on the hill of Ayasuluk in Selçuk, built over the place where Christians honored the tomb of John the Apostle. A small memorial church stood there by the 4th century; in the 6th century the emperor Justinian replaced it with a great domed basilica.

callouts.label: İsa Bey Mosque
callouts.hint: A square building at the foot of the far hill, just below the church.
callouts.description: The İsa Bey Mosque was built in 1375 for İsa Bey, a ruler of the Aydınid beylik, one of the Turkish states that held this coast before the Ottomans. Its builders reused granite columns from ancient Ephesus, the same habit of reuse we read on every site.

callouts.label: Temple of Artemis
callouts.hint: A small rectangle inside a large pale precinct on the plain, below the far hill.
callouts.description: The Temple of Artemis, the Artemision, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The first great marble temple was begun around 550 BCE; after a fire in 356 BCE it was rebuilt on the same huge plan. Today one column has been re-erected in a marshy field, and its sculptures are in the British Museum.
callouts.tip: Each column stood about 18 meters tall, the height of a six-story building.

callouts.label: Byzantine City Walls
callouts.hint: A dark line drawn close around the northern part of the city, much tighter than the outer wall.
callouts.description: The Byzantine City Walls are a later, much shorter circuit built in the early Byzantine period, probably the 7th century CE, when plague, earthquakes, and raids had shrunk the city. They enclose only the area around the harbor, the theater, and the Church of Mary.
callouts.tip: Compare the two wall lines on the sign: the short Byzantine wall shows how much smaller the city had become.

callouts.label: Vedius Gymnasium
callouts.hint: A square building at the north end of the city, beside the stadium.
callouts.description: The Vedius Gymnasium was a bath and exercise complex given to the city around 150 CE by a rich citizen, Publius Vedius Antoninus, and his wife, Flavia Papiane. Wealthy families paid for public buildings like this one to win honor, the same habit that produced the Library of Celsus.

callouts.label: Damianus Stoa / Via Sacra
callouts.hint: A road running northeast from the city toward the temple on the plain.
callouts.description: The Via Sacra, the sacred way, linked the city to the Temple of Artemis. In the 2nd century CE a wealthy teacher of speaking, Titus Flavius Damianus, paid for a long covered colonnade along it, the Damianus Stoa, so that worshippers could walk to the goddess in any weather.
callouts.tip: The number 22 appears twice on the sign, once on each road that joined the city to the temple.

callouts.label: Stadium
callouts.hint: A long building with one rounded end, set against the northern hill.
callouts.description: The Stadium was the city's racetrack, first laid out in the Hellenistic period and rebuilt under Nero in the 1st century CE. It held footraces and athletic games, and later gladiator fights and animal hunts. Much of its stone was later carried off for other buildings.

callouts.label: Cemetery of the Seven Sleepers
callouts.hint: A small marked site on the eastern side of the northern hill, outside the city.
callouts.description: The Cemetery of the Seven Sleepers is a burial ground and church built over caves on the east side of Panayırdağ. Legend says seven young Christians hid in a cave here during a persecution around 250 CE, fell asleep, and woke about two hundred years later in a Christian empire. The Quran tells a version of the same story as the People of the Cave.
callouts.tip: The story is a legend, but the cemetery is real: hundreds of graves were dug here because people wanted to be buried near the holy cave.

callouts.label: State Agora
callouts.hint: A long open square with buildings along its north side, near an information point in the upper city.
callouts.description: The State Agora is the square where the city's government did its business. On its north side stood the Basilica Stoa, a long hall built under Augustus with bulls' heads on its Ionic capitals, and beside it the small Odeon, a roofed hall for the city council, and the Prytaneion, the town hall where the sacred flame of the city burned.
callouts.tip: Look for the bulls' heads on the Basilica Stoa capitals. Chapter 10 uses one of these columns to teach the parts of a classical column.

callouts.label: East Gymnasium
callouts.hint: A square walled building just inside the southeast gate, at the upper end of the street grid.
callouts.description: The East Gymnasium is a large Roman bath and exercise complex built in the 2nd century CE just inside the Magnesian Gate. A Roman gymnasium was more than a gym: young men trained in its courtyard, attended lectures, and finished in the heated baths. It is sometimes called the Girls' Gymnasium after statues of girls found in it.

callouts.label: Magnesian Gate
callouts.hint: A gate symbol at the southeast corner of the city wall, where a road leaves the city toward the plain.
callouts.description: The Magnesian Gate is the eastern gate in the city wall, where the road from Magnesia on the Maeander and the sacred road from the Temple of Artemis entered Ephesus. It was built with the Hellenistic walls and rebuilt in Roman times. Processions carrying the images of Artemis came in here, and most tours begin near it, at the upper entrance, so the walk through the city runs downhill.
callouts.tip: Start here and walk downhill. The numbers 1 to 12 roughly follow the route most groups take, from the upper gate to the theater and Harbor Street.

callouts.label: Çukuriçi Höyük (Prehistoric Settlement)
callouts.hint: A marker in a different shape on the open plain, south of the city.
callouts.description: Çukuriçi Höyük is a prehistoric settlement mound southeast of Ephesus, first lived in around 6700 BCE, more than eight thousand years ago, and occupied on and off into the Early Bronze Age. Its farmers and metal workers were here thousands of years before Artemis or Lysimachus.
callouts.tip: The different marker shape on the sign sets it apart: it is the oldest place on the map.
